Article Title: 'When down, Manisha sher ki tarah jhapatta maarti hai': How Bhanwala overturned 0-6 deficit to win historic gold at World Championships
Article Text:
Manisha Bhanwala taking a victory lap after winning gold medal at the Senior World Wrestling Championships

NEW DELHI:

Manisha Bhanwala (L) in action against USA’s Abigail Nette in the Senior Wrestling World Championships final. (UWW)

My father has taught me one thing since childhood. If you get involved in any work, then finish it. That thing is in my blood Manisha Bhanwala

Path to LA 2028 and shift to 57kg category

Manisha Bhanwala became the first Indian woman wrestler to win gold at the World Championships. (UWW)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

An athlete’s biggest test, perhaps, comes not when they’re dominating but when they’re down. When a match is going against them. When the clock is against them. When a glance at the scoreboard doesn’t give reason to breathe easy, Manisha Bhanwala, competing in the non-Olympic 59kg category, faced multiple challenges in the Wrestling World Championships final on Friday.At Astana’s Barys Arena, USA’s Abigail Nette led Bhanwala 6-0 in the first period and then 6-1 at the break. But a lapse from the American gave the 29-year-old Indian an ‘in’ which saw the deficit reduced to two points. With half a minute left, Bhanwala forced a takedown to take an 8-6 lead, which she held on to win a historic gold medal.How historic? Manisha Bhanwala had become the first Indian woman to win a gold medal at the Wrestling World Championships. She became the first Indian, male or female, to stand atop the podium since Sushil Kumar in 2010. At 29, she is the oldest of the 24 Indians to have won a medal at the World Championships.However, none of this would have been possible without the mental strength to overturn that 0-6 deficit.“Manisha and I sat and watched her (Nette) videos before the final. We observed that she gets tired in the fifth or sixth minute. After that, she would get exhausted.But, as a coach, as a guardian, there was a tiny bit of concern at 0-6,” said national coach Virender Kumar in a virtual interaction conducted by Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) from Astana on Saturday.“Still, I was confident that in these moments, Manisha starts to pounce like a lion. I knew she would take a lot of points in the fifth minute. She has the capability to take 10 points in a minute. In the 30-second break, I told Manisha that she would take a lot of points in the fifth or sixth minute. I was confident of it,” he continued.The seeds for such confidence and mental strength are sown in training. In sparring contests, she would experiment with different scenarios to keep herself ready for competitions: down 0-6, as was the case in the final, down 0-10 and other such virtual situations.Manisha took up wrestling late in her life, introduced to it by her late father Suresh, who she still fondly refers to as "Father Sahab".Born in Siwaha, 10 km outside Jind in Haryana, Manisha took up wrestling to please her father. As Manisha held the tricolour aloft and wore the gold medal around her neck, her father was with her.She wore a special t-shirt bearing his photograph during her warm-up. Prior to leaving for Kazakhstan, she got a white T-shirt printed and had the faces of her parents added to it."There is no 'idea' behind this. These things cannot be 'ideas'. These are feelings, something you just get from the inside. Three days before arriving in Astana, I got it done. I got it done because I had a feeling that I would come back with a medal, with a record," said Manisha.With brother Rinku a kabaddi player and sister-in-law Mamta Sihag a wrestler, the family knows a thing or two about heartbreak. None bigger than when Suresh passed away due to a cardiac arrest shortly before Manisha was set to leave for the 2022 Asian Championships in Mongolia.A distraught Manisha wished to skip the competition but her family reminded her of Suresh's dreams. Eventually, Manisha won a bronze medal there before adding three more Asian Championships medals, including a gold last year."My father has taught me one thing since childhood. If you get involved in any work, then finish it. That thing is in my blood. Don't get involved in any work if you don't plan on finishing it. For me, the first and last option is wrestling," said Manisha.Coach Virender Kumar stressed her work ethic and dedication to the sport. "When I met Manisha for the first time in 2022, I was her junior coach. In the summers of May and June, the temperature was around 45 degrees. When she used to go for practise, she used to do it twice a day. At that time, I used to think, ‘Is this girl crazy?’”“Then, gradually, I got attached to her. This girl has no hobby, no interest in going out and watching movies, spend money on clothes, etc. She has only one hobby: wrestling. And the result of that is in front of you," he continued.The big challenge for Manisha now is the shift to the 57kg category with the aim of not just qualifying for LA 2028 but winning a medal too. Having competed in multiple categories - 59kg, 57kg, 62kg, 65kg - Manisha's big challenge will be to maintain weight for the 57kg competition."When I won yesterday (Friday), the coach came in the evening. The whole team was there. The coach decided that training begins from the morning itself. Now we have the senior nationals and the PWL (Pro Wrestling League). When the India camp starts, we will start from there. The whole team will work on it. We will then reassess what to do, which competitions to play, and which not to play. The coach decides after speaking to the rest of the team," said Manisha.Coach Virender Kumar said Manisha can count on her wealth of experience when it comes to this highly competitive category."As a team member, there are more girls in 57kg. But after a year, the biggest thing will be the experience. If yesterday there was another girl in place of Manisha, who was trailing 0-6 in the final, I don't think she would have recovered from it."I will give an example. Look at Kajal, she is 18 years old. She lost the final that she should have won. The only reason she lost was that she's inexperienced. In the next year and more, what Manisha does in domestic and international season will be key, but so will be the experience," he finished.
Article Summary: Manisha Bhanwala became the first Indian woman wrestler to win gold at the World Championships. The 29-year-old Indian took up wrestling late in her life, introduced to it by her late father Suresh, who she still fondly refers to as "Father Sahab". At 29, she is the oldest of the 24 Indians to have won a medal at the world championships.

Article Title: Dhruv Jurel's unbeaten 99 rescues India A after dramatic collapse against New Zealand A
Article Text:
Dhruv Jurel (AFP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Dhruv Jurel led India's fightback with a determined unbeaten 99 after the visitors suffered a dramatic collapse on the opening day of the second unofficial Test against New Zealand A in Christchurch.Coming into the match after scores of 1 and 2 in the first unofficial Test last week, Jurel responded with a crucial knock that helped India A recover from a precarious position and finish the day with a fighting total.India A were in trouble in the afternoon session after losing three wickets for just six runs in the space of six deliveries. At 160 for 6, with a substantial part of the day's play still remaining, Jurel took charge and first stitched together a 62-run partnership for the seventh wicket with Manav Suthar.After Suthar departed for 22, Jurel continued to hold the innings together, adding an unbeaten 69 runs with Akash Deep. He reached the 90s in the 79th over but chose to remain unbeaten at 99, seeing out the final nine overs until stumps.The visitors had made a steady start despite challenging batting conditions. Yashasvi Jaiswal was dismissed for a duck just four deliveries into the day, trapped lbw by Fraser Sheat, whose late movement troubled the Indian batters throughout the innings.Sai Sudharsan, promoted to open in the absence of KL Rahul, and Devdutt Padikkal then steadied the innings. The pair negotiated the remainder of the opening session, with Sai Sudharsan surviving a couple of close calls against Sheat before settling into his innings.Padikkal, who had scored 199 in the opening game, initially struggled to get going but gradually found his rhythm through a series of fluent drives. He also adjusted his position at the crease to counter the movement, while punishing the shorter deliveries. A cut behind point brought up his half-century in the second session.Sai Sudharsan, meanwhile, looked set for a substantial contribution before edging at a delivery outside off from Jarrod McKay shortly after lunch. His dismissal opened the door for New Zealand A to take control.Sheat led the charge as India A lost three more wickets in quick succession. Padikkal chopped one back onto his stumps, R Smaran, playing his first match of the tour, was trapped lbw first ball after misjudging the movement, while Washington Sundar was beaten by a full delivery.With the innings in danger of falling apart, Jurel had to negotiate the movement and bounce offered by the Christchurch surface. As the seamers began to tire and strayed towards his pads, he found opportunities to score and gradually shifted the momentum.New Zealand A eventually turned to left-arm spinner Jayden Lennox, who was introduced to test Jurel in a batting line-up dominated by right-handers. However, the wicketkeeper-batter used his feet and the crease effectively, mixing sweeps with cuts and dabs to keep the scoreboard moving.Suthar provided valuable support before falling for 22 while attempting a drive off Lennox. Jurel then took responsibility for the lower order, ensuring India A avoided a repeat of their batting struggles in the first innings of the Lincoln match.His unbeaten 99 has given the visitors a measure of stability heading into the second day, with Akash Deep still alongside him at the crease.India A 291 for 7 (Jurel 99*, Padikkal 80, Sheat 4-50) vs New Zealand A
Article Summary: India A lost three wickets for just six runs in the space of six deliveries. Jurel took charge and stitched together a 62-run partnership for the seventh wicket with Manav Suthar. He reached the 90s in the 79th over but chose to remain unbeaten at 99.

Article Title: ‘If you want to fit Vaibhav’: Ex-India cricketer's message to Gautam Gambhir-led management on accommodating Sooryavanshi
Article Text:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Sanju Samson and Gautam Gambhir (BCCI Photo)

Poll Vote & Share your view Who should be dropped to make way for Vaibhav Sooryavanshi? Sanju Samson Abhishek Sharma 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Former India wicketkeeper Dinesh Karthik believes Abhishek Sharma should be rested rather than Sanju Samson being dropped again if India want to bring teenage batter Vaibhav Sooryavanshi back into the playing XI for the fifth and final T20I against New Zealand.Sooryavanshi missed the fourth T20I in Auckland after Ishan Kishan recovered from the injury that had ruled him out of the previous two matches. The youngster had made an impression in his last appearance, smashing 45 off just 19 balls in the third T20I in Wellington, but did not feature in Friday's match despite India having already secured the series.Karthik feels Samson should not repeatedly be the one making way whenever India look to accommodate Sooryavanshi. Speaking on Cricbuzz, he suggested giving Abhishek a break instead."I know the world will want Vaibhav to play. If they want to play Vaibhav, it has got to be in place of Abhishek, to give him a break, and that is how it should be. Every time there is anything related to Vaibhav, it is always Sanju. If you want to really fit in Vaibhav, Abhishek can take a break. The key word here is break," Karthik said.Samson started the series on a strong note, scoring a match-winning 67 off 33 balls in Christchurch to claim the Player of the Match award.However, he managed scores of 14 and 18 in the following two matches. He was also moved to No. 3 in the third T20I to make room for Sooryavanshi.The debate over India's batting combination comes after their 87-run defeat in the fourth T20I. New Zealand posted a formidable 259/7, courtesy of Glenn Phillips' 107 off 49 balls, before Jacob Duffy's four-wicket haul helped restrict India to 172/9.India have already clinched the five-match series 3-1, with the final T20I offering another opportunity to assess their combinations ahead of the next assignment.
Article Summary: Former India wicketkeeper Dinesh Karthik believes Abhishek Sharma should be rested rather than Sanju Samson. India have already clinched the five-match series 3-1. Sooryavanshi missed the fourth T20I in Auckland after Ishan Kishan recovered from an injury.

Article Title: 'What a fighter': Shikhar Dhawan celebrates Manisha Bhanwala's historic gold at Senior World Championships
Article Text:
Manisha Bhanwala

Manisha scripts history with stunning comeback in final

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

'What a fighter'

Manisha's impressive run to the gold medal

From a six-point deficit to standing atop the world podium, Manisha Bhanwala scripted a historic chapter in Indian wrestling with a stunning comeback victory in the women's 59kg final at the Senior World Championships in Astana, Kazakhstan. Her remarkable triumph drew congratulations from across the sporting fraternity, with former India cricketer Shikhar Dhawan leading the praise for the wrestler's fighting spirit.Manisha produced an extraordinary turnaround against Nette on Friday, overturning a six-point deficit to secure an 8-6 victory and deliver India's maiden gold medal in the history of the Senior World Championships.The Indian wrestler endured a difficult start as Nette established a 5-0 advantage through a four-point throw and an additional point following India's unsuccessful challenge. A subsequent caution against Manisha extended the American's lead to 6-0, leaving the Indian with a mountain to climb.However, Manisha refused to surrender and opened her account with a stepout point before the break. She carried that momentum into the second period, executing a takedown to reduce the deficit.Another unsuccessful challenge from the American corner handed Manisha an additional point and an opportunity to attack from par terre.She capitalised with a two-point gut-wrench to level the scores at 6-6 before delivering the decisive pressure takedown to move ahead 8-6.Manisha then held her ground against Nette's attempts to regain the advantage, completing a memorable comeback to secure the gold medal.Dhawan lauded Manisha for refusing to give up after falling 0-6 behind against the USA's Abigail Nette, eventually producing an 8-6 victory to become the first Indian to win a gold medal at the Senior World Championships.“From 0-6 down to becoming a World Champion! What a fighter, Manisha! You’ve made the entire nation proud. Congratulations!,” Dhawan wrote on X.Her journey to the final was equally impressive. She began her campaign with a 6-2 victory over Canada's Laurence Beauregard in the pre-quarterfinals before overcoming Mongolia's Bolortuya Khurelkhuu in the semifinals to book her place in the gold-medal bout.Manisha's historic triumph also provided a major boost to India's campaign after the country endured disappointment in two other women's finals. Neelam in the 50kg category and Kajal in the 76kg category had to settle for silver medals.
Article Summary: Manisha Bhanwala produced an extraordinary turnaround against the USA's Abigail Nette. She overturned a six-point deficit to secure an 8-6 victory and deliver India's maiden gold medal in the history of the Senior World Championships. Former India cricketer Shikhar Dhawan led the praise for the wrestler's fighting spirit.

Article Title: Ranji Trophy: Tanush Kotian takes career-best 8-81 as Mumbai secure third bonus point win
Article Text:
Mumbai's Tanush Kotian raises the ball in the air as he greets spectators after taking a five-wicket haul with a total of 8 wickets in the second innings

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view What factor contributed most to Mumbai's victory? Kotian's bowling Raghuvanshi's batting Strong teamwork 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Mumbai: Off-spinner Tanush Kotian produced a career-best 8-81 and an impressive match haul of 11-151 as Mumbai crushed Haryana by 10 wickets on the fourth and final day of their Ranji Trophy Elite Group D clash at the MCA ground.The win gave Mumbai their third successive bonus-point victory of the season, marking their best start in a long time. They now have 21 points from three matches - the most among all teams in the Ranji Trophy - and sit atop their group, firmly placed on the road to the knockouts.Mumbai will next take on Railways at the Brabourne Stadium at the Cricket Club of India from November 2-5.The match will remain special for Kotian, who was playing his 50th first-class game. He marked the occasion with his first 10-wicket match haul and his fourth five-wicket haul.Chasing a modest target of 97, Mumbai openers Angkrish Raghuvanshi and Divyaansh Saxena completed the job in just 10.4 overs. Raghuvanshi, riding high after scoring his maiden first-class century in the first innings, smashed an unbeaten 67 off 39 balls. Saxena, who had struggled in his previous two innings, made a confidence-boosting 30 not out off 25 balls.The final day, however, was not entirely straightforward for Mumbai. Haryana's eighth-wicket pair of Samant Jakhar and Anuj Thakral made the hosts toil on a slow surface, adding 81 runs over nearly two hours.Kotian eventually broke the stand by bowling Jakhar. Haryana, who had resumed on 73-2, still 87 runs behind after following on, were bowled out for 256 in the second session.Reflecting on Mumbai's strong start to the season, Kotian said, "As a team, we've worked well. It's very difficult to get a third victory with a bonus point. Everyone is backing each other and giving confidence. We're trying to contribute together. If the team goal is going well, we want to keep moving forward like this."Brief scores: Mumbai 430 & 97-0 (Raghuvanshi 67*). Haryana 270 & (following-on) 256 (Kotian 8-81) Mumbai won by 10 wickets. Points: Mumbai 7, Haryana 0.
Article Summary: Mumbai beat Haryana by 10 wickets in their Ranji Trophy Elite Group D clash. Off-spinner Tanush Kotian took a career-best 8-81 and an impressive match haul of 11-151. Mumbai openers Angkrish Raghuvanshi and Divyaansh Saxena completed the job in 10.4 overs.

Article Title: Roman Reigns inspired his punches; Andre Russell earned him a nickname: Meet Army havaldar and Asian Games medallist Kapil Pokhariya
Article Text:
Kapil Pokhariya's fascination with pro-wrestler Roman Reigns was well known in his locality. (Image credit: Special arrangement)

From Khatima to the Asian Games podium

Kapil Pokhariya with his father (Image credit: Special arrangement)

From a small training ground to the boxing ring

Kapil Pokhariya (Image credit: Special arrangement)

Kapil Pokhariya (Image credit: Special arrangement)

The ‘ Andre Russell ’ of Khatima

Kapil Pokhariya (Image credit: Special arrangement)

The Road Ahead and LA 2028 Dream

NEW DELHI: Jumping on cotton-filled mattresses, punching pillows, throwing them over walls and hitting a homemade punching bag filled with mountain soil - Kapil Pokhariya’s childhood was all about pro-wrestling.His fascination with pro-wrestler Roman Reigns was well known in his locality. He would skip meals, playtime, and outings to watch WWE programming on television. Once the show was over, he would try to copy the moves and punches at home.Little did he know that this childhood fascination could one day bring him his biggest recognition.Today, Kapil - an Indian Army havaldar - is an Asian Games medallist. Kapil won bronze in the men’s 90kg boxing event at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.“I never knew that copying Roman Reigns and practising those punches would bring me this far. I used to save recordings of his videos, and I still have them. I am really proud of where I am today. Honestly, I started learning how to throw punches by copying Roman Reigns (laugh),” Kapil told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview."My favourite was WrestleMania and Money in the Bank," he said.Kapil hails from Chakarpur village in Khatima, Uttarakhand, far from the major boxing centres that have produced several Indian stars.His father, Narendra Singh Pokhariya, served in the Indian Army. He wanted his son to study well and join the Army as a commissioned officer. Boxing, however, was never part of the original plan.Narendra often watched his son copy WWE stars at home. Initially, he would scold and even beat him for damaging things around the house. But his view slowly changed when he saw Kapil putting sand into a thick sack after returning from school and punching it with all his strength.“A teacher used to teach boxing at a nearby school. I saw the students punching a bag and decided to make one myself. My father scolded me in the beginning, but later he took me to a training centre and got me admitted there. That is how I got into boxing,” Kapil said.Kapil did not begin his boxing journey at a big academy. His first steps came at a small training ground, where he practised alongside boys of his age and those who were older. After a few months, he began training under a coach.“I come from a small village where boxing was never a popular sport. Pooran Bohra sir was there. He trained a small group of boys for just a few hours on selected days of the week. But I was interested in learning. I listened to him carefully and repeated everything he taught me when I returned home,” Kapil said.With time, Kapil developed as a boxer and competed in his first state-level competition in 2015. He went into the tournament with excitement but came away disappointed. His first competitive bout ended in defeat in the opening round.“I was really disappointed. It was the first bout of my life, and I was seeing such a large crowd for the first time. I lost in the first round. But that competition and the defeat taught me a lot. My interest in boxing grew even stronger after that,” he said.Kapil returned with a different mindset at the national-level competition. This time, he did more than win his bouts - he also claimed the gold medal. The prize money was followed by a job in the Indian Army. He joined the force in April 2017 and was appointed as a havaldar. His boxing career took a big step forward after that.The Army gave him opportunities to improve his skills and compete at a higher level. He began training more seriously, took part in Services competitions, won medals and continued to grow as a boxer.“My father wanted me to study and join the Army as a commissioned officer. He joined as a sepoy and retired as a havaldar. But he wanted me to reach a higher rank if I joined the Indian Army,” Kapil said.“He was very happy. The day I won a national medal, he hugged me. That was when I realised that I had achieved something big in my life,” Kapil said.“Now, after winning this Asian Games medal, I will be promoted to naib subedar. Papa said, ‘Ab tu mera senior ho gaya hai’,” the Indian boxer recalled with a smile.Like many children in India, Kapil also grew up playing gully cricket. He even played inter-village cricket in Uttarakhand.His height, muscular build and powerful hitting made him a popular figure on the local cricket grounds. His ability to hit big sixes earned him the nickname ‘Russell’, after West Indies power-hitter Andre Russell.“I loved Andre Russell. I also liked Hardik Pandya. People used to call me ‘Khatima ka Russell’ because of my power. The boys wanted me in their team because I could hit big sixes,” he said, laughing.For Kapil, the Asian Games bronze is only the beginning. His biggest dream is to represent India at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics and win a medal.Under the Boxing Federation of India's selection criteria, Asian Games medallists will be selected as the main entries in their respective weight categories for the 2027 World Boxing Championships in Astana, Kazakhstan. The tournament is scheduled for April and will be the first qualifying event in boxing for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.Kapil knows there is still a long road ahead. “Rukna nahi hai ab, bas aage dekhna hai,” he said.“The Olympics is the ultimate dream. I want to go there, represent my country and win a medal. That is the only thing on my mind right now. I am preparing for the World Championships in April,” he added.
Article Summary: Kapil Pokhariya won bronze in the men’s 90kg boxing event at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. Kapil hails from Chakarpur village in Khatima, Uttarakhand, far from the major boxing centres that have produced several Indian stars. His fascination with pro-wrestler Roman Reigns was well known in his locality.

Article Title: Asian Champions Trophy Hockey: India look to continue winning run against China
Article Text:
Image credit: Hockey India

Mandeep makes a strong statement

Fulton wants India to improve after the break

China present a different challenge

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Other Asian Champions Trophy matches on Thursday

Match Start time Malaysia vs South Korea 2.30 pm Japan vs Bangladesh 4.45 pm India vs China 7 pm

India squad

India will look to build on their strong start to the Asian Champions Trophy when they face China in their second round-robin match on Thursday. The five-time champions began their title defence with a big win over Bangladesh and will be keen to maintain their momentum against a young Chinese side.India, who recently won their second successive Asian Games gold medal to secure direct qualification for the Los Angeles Olympics, dominated Bangladesh in their opening match. Bangladesh replaced Pakistan in the tournament after the latter refused to travel to India, citing security reasons.The match was largely played in Bangladesh's half, with India controlling the contest. While Bangladesh were not expected to pose a major challenge, India's ability to score from both field play and penalty corners was an encouraging sign.The Harmanpreet Singh-led side scored eight field goals and five goals from set pieces against Bangladesh on Tuesday.Veteran forward Mandeep Singh was among the standout performers, scoring a hat-trick. His return to form comes at an important time, with national selectors expected to assess the players after the tournament.Mandeep was reportedly among four senior players who could be phased out after the ACT.The other three were Jarmanpreet Singh, Amit Rohidas and Nilakanta Sharma.Nilakanta announced on Tuesday that the tournament would be his last at the international level. However, Mandeep and Jarmanpreet are keen to continue playing.Apart from Mandeep's three goals, captain Harmanpreet, Dilpreet Singh and vice-captain Hardik Singh scored twice each. Shilanand Lakra, Nilakanta and Jugraj Singh also got on the scoresheet.India chief coach Craig Fulton was pleased with Mandeep's performance."He (Mandeep) was good, he did full of running and was nice and sharp, which was important," he said.Despite the convincing result, Fulton felt India needed to perform better in the third quarter, after the teams changed ends."We wanted a fast start, which we got in the first quarter. We wanted to play some fast-flowing hockey, which we did. But the third quarter wasn't that good, and that remains a problem. But I am glad we finished strongly," he pointed out.India had to manage without midfielder Manpreet Singh, who has been ruled out of the tournament because of a calf muscle injury. Hardik, Vivek Sagar Prasad and Nilakanta took charge of the midfield against Bangladesh and combined well with the forwards.Mandeep was a major threat in attack, with Abhishek, Dilpreet, Shilanand and Sukhjeet Singh supporting him.At the back, Harmanpreet, Amit Rohidas, Jugraj and Sanjay will continue to shoulder responsibility, while Suraj Karkera and Krishan Bahadur Pathak are the goalkeeping options.India will face a less familiar opponent in China, who pushed Asian Games silver medallists Malaysia hard before going down 4-5 in their opening match.China have brought an entirely new squad for the tournament, with their young players showing promise against Malaysia. Their lack of recent exposure against India, however, makes them a difficult team to assess.Fulton admitted that India had limited information about their opponents."This Chinese team is unknown to us, as they have come here with a completely new group, not the one that played at the Asian Games. We don't know much about them and haven't seen them play. We will have to analyse video footage of their match to get a fair idea about them," Fulton said.India will aim to carry their attacking form into Thursday's match while addressing the concerns raised by their coach. China, meanwhile, will look to build on their close contest against Malaysia and challenge the defending champions.Malaysia will face South Korea, while Japan will take on Bangladesh in the other matches scheduled for Thursday.Goalkeepers: Suraj Karkera, Krishan Bahadur PathakDefenders: Sanjay, Harmanpreet Singh (captain), Amit Rohidas, Jugraj Singh, Jarmanpreet Singh, Amandeep LakraMidfielders: Rajinder Singh, Aditya Arjun Lalage, Nilakanta Sharma, Hardik Singh, Vivek Sagar PrasadForwards: Shilanand Lakra, Abhishek, Sukhjeet Singh, Dilpreet Singh, Mandeep Singh
Article Summary: India will face China in their second round-robin match on Thursday. The five- time champions began their title defence with a big win over Bangladesh. Harmanpreet Singh-led side scored eight field goals and five goals from set pieces against Bangladesh.

Article Title: Nagaland United to add a new chapter to Talimeren Ao’s legacy by becoming first club from Nagaland on national stage with IFL debut
Article Text:
NUSC Stadium (left) and Talimeren Ao

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

On the 107th anniversary of independent India’s first captain, Talimeren Ao, on Jan 28 last year, a new football stadium was inaugurated at the foothills of the Naga Hills in Chümoukedima, and a one-year-old club from the municipality played its first competitive match.Nagaland United FC lost that game 2-3 to Barak FC but wrote a new chapter in the football fate of the state that had given India the skipper who led the country from the front barefoot at the 1948 Olympics in London, carrying with him a nascent nation’s hopes in its first international campaign.And, on a chilly evening in Srinagar on Friday, Nagaland United will continue that legacy, albeit after a gap of 78 years, when they take on hosts Real Kashmir in the Indian Football League opener at TRC Stadium and become the first club to represent the northeastern state on the national stage.“Our aim in our debut IFL season is to build a competitive, disciplined, and fearless team that represents Nagaland with pride,” coach Kaizad Ambapardiwalla told TOI. “We want to compete strongly in every match, establish our identity through attacking football, high intensity, and teamwork, and challenge ourselves against the best teams in the league.”This promotion of a two-year-old club into the second-tier competition was courtesy of another club from the region that stamped its authority at the top tier by winning the I-League in 2017 – Aizawl FC.Having won their first tournament in October last year with the NSF Martyrs’ Memorial Trophy title, the club from Chümoukedima got the chance to face Aizawl FC on June 6, who came calling to their neighbours under the banner of Football for Peace and a “Match for Peace, Goal for Hope”.The visitors won that game 2-0, but three months later, on September 9, the All India Football Federation approved a goodwill agreement for Nagaland United to take a cash-strapped Aizawl’s place in the IFL, as the Mizoram club pledged technical and development support.Taking on the baton from a former I-League champion that has represented northeast for eleven straight seasons in the national league without relegation, Nagaland United will look to add another chapter in the football history of Nagaland, but of the football-loving northeast.“For me, it’s more than just playing at a higher level: it’s an opportunity to give back to the club that gave me my start, represent my state with pride, and hopefully inspire the young players back home to believe that their dreams, too, are possible,” 19-year-old Nagaland United defender Thejangulie Zatsu told TOI.“I know my journey is far from over, and I just want to keep growing, give everything I have for this badge, and make everyone who has believed in me proud.”On the evening of October 30, across Nagaland, people will gather around the screens: in community halls, in living rooms, in shops with their shutters half down as Nagaland FC get the opportunity to add another chapter to the story that started a hundred years ago with a Naga boy chasing a pomelo across a mission playground in the Naga Hills.“As a defender myself, his journey means even more to me because I play in the same position (as Amo). It gives me something to look up to and reminds me that where we come from should never limit how far we can dream,” added Zatsu.Friday will see that dream continue its journey from the foot of the Naga Hills to the Himalayan valley in Kashmir.
Article Summary: Nagaland United FC will play in the Indian Football League for the first time in 78 years on Friday. The two-year-old club will take on hosts Real Kashmir at TRC Stadium in Srinagar. Nagaland will become the first club from the northeastern state to represent India on the national stage.

Article Title: ISL: An attacking contest on card as leaders NEUFC lock horns with Bengaluru FC

KOLKATA: Still unbeaten after three matches, despite the frustrating stalemate away in their last game, NorthEast United FC will be back on Friday to continue their winning run at home and stay at the top of the Indian Super League table.“The mentality. We go into every game with the mentality that we are no longer the underdogs,” head coach Juan Pedro Benali said at the pre-match interaction on Thursday.However, on the other half of the field at Indira Gandhi Athletic Stadium in Guwahati, will be a side that is also unbeaten in their ISL campaign and sit on the fourth spot having played one game less than the hosts.When NEUFC take on Bengaluru FC , it will be a test of the Highlanders’ defensive solidity – having conceded just one goal in three games – against the attacking prowess of the visitors, led by India striker Ryan Williams.NEUFC were held to a goalless draw by Odisha FC in their previous outing, with striker Alaaeddine Ajaraie missing a stoppage-time penalty, while Bengaluru registered a 2-0 win over Chennaiyin FC through goals from Williams and Mihailo Perovic.Benali believes that the challenge for NEUFC will be as much about breaking down Bengaluru’s structure as it will be about managing their attacking threats.“The details, concentration and crucial phases of the game will make the difference,” Benali added, underlining the fine margins that could decide the final scoreline.NorthEast United, meanwhile, will look to use their own attacking options and vary their approach to create openings. And, despite Ajaraie’s late penalty miss against Odisha FC in the last game, the Spanish coach kept his faith in the skills of their Moroccan talisman.“I prefer to win 4-3. I don’t want 0-0. I want to win. If there is a penalty tomorrow, Ajaraie will take it. There is no doubt about it,” Benali made it clear.Bengaluru coach Pep Munoz is also aware of the Ajaraie threat to their defence on the day.“They have an identity, some patterns that they like to create and a clear style of play,” Munoz said on Thursday, adding that his team is prepared to face either a back-four or a back-five defensive system.Going into the match after a break, Bengaluru will also hope to keep up their winning run as the fixture looks destined for an exciting contest of attack and defence for the fans.
Article Summary: NorthEast United FC take on Bengaluru FC in the Indian Super League on Friday. The Highlanders are unbeaten after three games and sit top of the table. Article Title: 'Enjoying the game has to be the fundamental,' says Tvesa Malik after top-10 finish at India Open
Article Text:
Tvesa Malik (TOI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: For Tvesa Malik, a strong performance at the Women’s Indian Open was as much about mastering her mind as it was about getting her golf right. The Indian golfer finished seventh at the DLF Golf and Country Club in Gurugram, carding a four-round total of one-under 287 (71, 73, 71, 72) to emerge as one of three Indians in the top 10. With Vani Kapoor finishing second and Pranavi Urs sharing fourth place, the home contingent enjoyed an encouraging week at the event.“I think everyone can see it. I’ve always been really proud of how, despite how small the Women’s Golf Association of India (WGAI) started out and how few girls have been playing, so many have gone on to play in Europe and overseas. It’s not an easy standard,” said Tvesa.The progress, she added, has been building for years, with Aditi Ashok establishing herself internationally before Pranavi Urs and other Indian golfers delivered strong performances, including at the Asian Games. The recent Women’s Indian Open, she felt, was another encouraging sign of that development.The emergence of young talent has also caught her attention. Ojaswini Saraswat, who made the cut at the Women’s Indian Open at just 13, offered a glimpse of the potential among the next generation. For Tvesa, however, the key to nurturing young golfers is ensuring that the desire to play comes from within.“A lot of the time, it’s actually their parents who come and ask questions about how they should proceed.For me, it has always been about enjoying the game. That has to be the fundamental. If that is there, the sky is the limit,” she said.She added, “Parents have an important role in helping young players pursue their ambitions, but the goals must ultimately belong to the children themselves.”While younger players today have access to better information and are developing their games at an early age, Tvesa believes they must also learn to manage expectations. The competition is becoming younger and more intense, making it important to balance ambition with patience.Reflecting on Ojaswini’s achievement, she said, “You have to realize that you’re still so young and there’s so much time. Continue learning, ride that experience, and, at the same time, don’t set expectations so high that they become unrealistic.”Tvesa’s own performance at DLF was a reminder of the importance of that balance. The demanding course, known for punishing inaccurate shots and misplaced approaches, requires players to remain composed even when things do not go according to plan.While her ball-striking had been encouraging, she felt her mental approach made the bigger difference during the week.“This year, I felt a bit more accepting of the course. When you play there and you’re from there, the expectations are always high. It’s such a fine line between pushing yourself and almost holding yourself back,” she said.Tvesa, who is familiar with the DLF layout, explained that a single mistake can have a significant impact because of the course’s demanding nature. Accuracy off the tee and precise approach shots are crucial, while missing a green in the wrong place can make even saving par difficult.Her ability to accept those setbacks and move on was particularly encouraging. She recalled how her caddie praised her composure after the final round.“My caddie said the biggest thing was not actually what I had played, but the fact that I didn’t get upset. That impressed him the most,” she said.For Tvesa, patience was the key. Rather than allowing a mistake to affect the rest of her round, she reminded herself that more opportunities would come.That mental adjustment is also central to the challenge she is working to overcome in her professional career. Although she feels her technique has improved significantly, the results have not always reflected the quality of her game.Tvesa, who is married to fellow professional golfer Ajeetesh Sandhu, said, “Your technique is good enough when you’ve practiced and played for this long. Then you have to find the small things that give you an edge. Awareness is a big thing, understanding where I’m making mistakes and why, rather than just spending all my time working on technique,”.Beyond individual performance, Tvesa believes Indian women’s golf needs stronger institutional support to sustain its progress. Drawing on her experience competing on the Ladies European Tour, she pointed to systems in countries such as Sweden, Germany, and Australia, where players receive assistance with accommodation, coaching, physiotherapy, and training facilities.“It’s an expensive game to play, and support is necessary for everybody. Having a team around a player also provides mental reassurance when travel, fatigue, and changing conditions affect performance,” she said.
Article Summary: Tvesa Malik was one of three Indians in the top 10 at the Women's Indian Open. The Indian golfer finished seventh at the DLF Golf and Country Club in Gurugram. Vani Kapoor finished second and Pranavi Urs shared fourth place at the event.

Article Title: Mirabai Chanu pulls out of World Championships with back issue; Gyaneshwari Yadav finishes eighth

Commonwealth Games silver medallist Gyaneshwari Yadav finished eighth in the women's 53kg category at the IWF World Championships on Thursday, while India's star weightlifter Mirabai Chanu withdrew from the event due to a back issue.Gyaneshwari, 23, from Chhattisgarh, recorded a combined lift of 198kg, with 88kg in the snatch and 110kg in the clean and jerk, to finish on top of Group C. Her total was also better than those achieved by several lifters from Groups A and B.The Asian Championship silver medallist could have improved on her personal best of 199kg and secured a higher overall finish had she converted two missed attempts, one in each section.Chanu, meanwhile, was forced to pull out before making her much-anticipated debut in the 53kg category. She had been assigned to Group B with an entry total of 200kg but withdrew after experiencing back pain.China's Zhang Haiqin claimed the gold medal with a total of 221kg (98kg+123kg). American Eleanor Ulrey took silver with 220kg (98kg+122kg), while North Korea's So Hyon Kim secured bronze with 214kg (91kg+123kg).The snatch competition also saw seven lifters register lifts of at least 90kg, a benchmark Chanu has been working towards for more than six years.At the World Championships, lifters are divided into groups based on their declared entry totals, which represent the combined weight they intend to lift in the snatch and clean and jerk. Group A features those with the highest entry totals, followed by Groups B, C and D.The World Championships is among six events in the first phase of the qualification system for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

India will have a 17-member contingent, featuring 11 women and six men, competing across 11 sports at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Senegal from October 31 to November 13.Table tennis player Syndrela Das, badminton talent Tanvi Patri and swimmer Dhinidhi Desinghu are among the country's leading medal prospects at the fourth edition of the Summer Youth Olympics, which will be staged in Africa for the first time.Das will take part in the women's singles table tennis competition, while Asian Under-17 badminton champion Patri will represent India in the women's singles event. Desinghu is entered in three swimming events: the women's 100m freestyle, 200m freestyle and 200m individual medley.India's participation will span athletics, archery, badminton, beach wrestling, boxing, equestrian, judo, swimming, table tennis, windsurfing and wushu. The 17-athlete squad will be the country's smallest contingent at a Summer Youth Olympic Games.The 2026 edition will be held across Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly over 15 days. Around 2,700 athletes are expected to compete in 25 sports for 153 medal events. Ten additional engagement sports will also be part of the programme, but will not offer medals.Dakar 2026 will mark the first time an Olympic sporting event is held on African soil.The Games were initially scheduled for 2022 but were postponed by four years due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The previous Summer Youth Olympics took place in Buenos Aires, Argentina, in 2018.India have collected 23 medals across the three previous editions, comprising three gold, 16 silver and four bronze. The inaugural Games were held in Singapore in 2010, followed by Nanjing in China in 2014 and Buenos Aires in 2018.Organised by the International Olympic Committee (IOC), the Youth Olympic Games are designed for athletes primarily aged between 15 and 17. Alongside sporting competition, the event features educational and cultural programmes aimed at promoting Olympic values, participation and international understanding.The 2026 sports programme includes athletics, swimming, breaking, skateboarding, beach handball, beach wrestling, futsal, coastal rowing, Baseball5 and Wushu Taolu, among others. Baseball5 and Wushu Taolu will make their Youth Olympic Games debut. Ten engagement sports, including golf, karate and surfing, will be held without medal events.
Article Summary: India will have a 17-member contingent, featuring 11 women and six men, competing at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games. Table tennis player Syndrela Das, badminton talent Tanvi Patri and swimmer Dhinidhi Desinghu are among the country's leading medal prospects. The 2026 edition will be held across Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly over 15 days. Around 2,700 athletes are expected to compete in 25 sports for 153 medal events.

Former India opener Aakash Chopra has questioned India's decision to drop Vaibhav Sooryavanshi for the fourth T20I against New Zealand, urging the team management to clarify the youngster's role and long-term future in the side.Chopra felt Sooryavanshi should not be viewed merely as a stand-in whenever an established player is unavailable. He also suggested that if the teenager is unlikely to get regular opportunities in the playing XI, he would be better off returning to domestic cricket, particularly first-class cricket, to gain match experience and spend more time batting in the middle.Sooryavanshi got his opportunities in the second and third T20Is after Ishan Kishan was sidelined by an injury. He scored 4 and 45 in those two outings before making way for Kishan, who returned to the side for the fourth match.Chopra pointed out that the fourth T20I was a dead rubber and felt the decision to leave Sooryavanshi out raised questions about India's plans for the youngster."Last match, Abhishek made 100 and Vaibhav missed his 50. But the batting was very good. After that, the question was, if Ishan is fit, who will go out. If you think philosophically, then the answer is Vaibhav Sooryavanshi since he replaced an injured Kishan.But this was a dead rubber," Chopra said on his YouTube channel.He questioned whether Sooryavanshi would only feature when another player was unavailable, adding that regular cricket would be more beneficial if he was not part of India's immediate plans."The decision to drop Vaibhav Sooryavanshi leads to a bigger question. Will you play Vaibhav Sooryavanshi only when someone is injured? Or when someone is unavailable? If that is the case, you can send him home. You can tell him to go and play first-class cricket. Of course, he can learn by staying in the Indian dressing room. But if it's happening for an extended period, he should get bat on ball," he added.Chopra also called on the team management to make its thinking clear, saying that while a roadmap may already be in place, there has been little public clarity about Sooryavanshi's role."The team should come out and share what their roadmap and philosophy is. Maybe they have already thought about it and have already charted out a plan. But they haven't told anybody. As such, we don't know what they are going to do with Vaibhav Sooryavanshi. His absence was a little disappointing," Chopra said.Kishan, meanwhile, had a brief return to the side. He was dismissed for a duck as India failed to chase New Zealand's target of 260, eventually finishing at 172/9.
Article Summary: Former India opener Aakash Chopra questions India's decision to drop Vaibhav Sooryavanshi for the fourth T20I against New Zealand. Chopra suggested that if the teenager is unlikely to get regular opportunities, he should return to domestic cricket.

Article Title: 'I wanted to see my career out with Lancs': James Anderson reveals emotional toll of County exit
Article Text:
James Anderson (Photo by Reuters)

Anderson draws parallels between Lancashire and England exits

'Is there something fundamentally wrong with me?': Anderson opens up

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

James Anderson is still coming to terms with an unexpected end to his 25-year association with Lancashire, admitting that the county's decision not to renew his contract has left him questioning his future in cricket. The veteran fast bowler, who had hoped to finish his career at the club he supported as a child, said the experience brought back memories of how his England career came to an end nearly two years ago.The 44-year-old, speaking on the BBC podcast Tailenders, revealed that he has yet to decide whether to find another county or call time on his playing career. Despite the disappointment, Anderson said he was beginning to feel optimistic about the opportunities that lie ahead."I don't know what the end looks like, but obviously I wanted to see my career out with Lancs. I don't know if my career's done, we'll have to wait and see, but it'd be nice, at some point, if someone will let me retire," Anderson said."I'm still sort of trying to process everything, and weigh up what the best way forward for me is, really."Anderson's departure from Lancashire came as a surprise despite his impressive individual performances during the County Championship season.The veteran pacer captained the side and claimed 50 wickets, although Lancashire finished second-last in Division Two.Last month, the club's new director of cricket, Paul Farbrace, informed Anderson that his contract would not be renewed for the 2027 season. Reacting to the development, the fast bowler expressed his disappointment on Instagram, writing that "if it was up to me it wouldn't have ended like this."Anderson revealed that he had initially expected a discussion about Lancashire's performances and the team's plans for the future, rather than a conversation about his own departure."I went in for what I thought was a conversation about how the team moves forward, because obviously it wasn't a great year for the team," he said."Being captain, I thought it was sort of just a chat about that. And then a couple of minutes in, I realised it wasn't a conversation; I was just being told that they thought the best way for the team to move forward is without me. Obviously, I was quite shocked. It was quite brief and, yeah, that was it."The decision brought back memories of his England exit, when the team management informed him nearly two years ago that he was no longer part of their plans.The veteran pacer admitted that Lancashire's decision triggered self-doubt, particularly after he had spent the previous season trying to understand how he could help the team improve.Anderson said he had regularly discussed the team's struggles with the head coach and questioned whether there was anything more he could have done in his role as captain."Last year didn't go too well for us on the field and all the way through the season, myself and the head coach are like, 'Is it something we're doing? Could we be doing more to help the team play better?' I finished the season thinking, 'Was it something I did, but was I doing something wrong?'"And then I get told this news and then I'm thinking that even more. I'm thinking, 'God, this is happening again. Is there something fundamentally wrong with me as a person, as a human being?' But your head just sort of races. I just didn't really know what to make of it for a good week. You're thinking, 'God, I'm never going to play cricket again.' All these sorts of things."Anderson also made it clear that his emotional connection with Lancashire would remain unchanged despite the circumstances of his departure."I am sad the way it ended with the club I supported as a kid but now I have thought about it I am quite excited for the future. I am always going to support Lancashire."
Article Summary: Lancashire have decided not to renew James Anderson's contract. The fast bowler had hoped to finish his career at the club he supported as a child. The 44-year- old has yet to decide whether to find another county or call time on his playing career.

Article Title: 'It's win or lose': Ryan Rickelton predicts thrilling final-day finish in South Africa-Australia decider
Article Text:
South Africa's Ryan Rickelton (Image: AP/PTI)

Rickelton, Mulder hundreds power South Africa's fightback

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Rickelton warns Australia of challenging fourth-innings chase

With the series trophy, the No. 1 spot in the Test rankings and valuable World Test Championship (WTC) points on the line, South Africa and Australia are bracing for a high-stakes finish to their three-match series at Newlands. After a remarkable fightback from the hosts, the series-deciding third Test is delicately poised heading into the final day on Saturday, with South Africa wicketkeeper Ryan Rickelton ruling out the possibility of a stalemate."It's win or lose, I guess. No draw tomorrow. If you had to say that it's going down to the third Test, day five, with all three results on the cards or two results on the cards, yeah, I wouldn't have believed it. It's been a special series," Rickelton said, as quoted by cricinfo.Centuries from Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder helped South Africa recover from a precarious position and set Australia a challenging target of 288 runs to win the series-deciding third Test of the ICC World Test Championship 2025-27.Resuming their second innings at 140/4 on the fourth morning, the hosts eventually reached 387 before being bowled out in 134.4 overs, putting themselves in a strong position to push for a series victory.The foundation of South Africa's recovery was a magnificent 154-run partnership for the sixth wicket between Rickelton and Mulder. Rickelton struck 101 off 219 deliveries, while Mulder contributed 115 off 221 balls. Their stand is the second-highest sixth-wicket partnership by South Africa against Australia in Test cricket.Rickelton acknowledged that the new ball could present Australia with an opportunity to accelerate their chase, although the slow and deteriorating nature of the pitch could make the task considerably tougher."I just think with that new ball, there's obviously runs available, and there's obviously wickets too. It has been quite slow. If Australia obviously fancy having a go at it, it might just factor into it. For them to bat at effectively threes the whole day will be a big ask, especially on a slower, lower deteriorating wicket," he added.Earlier, South Africa were bowled out for 329 in their first innings before Australia responded with 429, taking a crucial 100-run lead. However, the hosts' second-innings resurgence has turned the contest on its head and left Australia with a challenging fourth-innings target.With the three-match series level at 1-1, both teams have everything to play for on the final day. Australia must chase down 288 to secure the series, while South Africa need 10 wickets to seal a memorable victory on home soil.
Article Summary: South Africa and Australia are bracing for a high-stakes finish to their three- match series at Newlands. The series-deciding third Test is delicately poised heading into the final day on Saturday. Australia must chase down 288 to secure the series, while South Africa need 10 wickets to seal a memorable victory.

Article Title: India's first women's Test 50 years ago: 22,000 fans, Shantha Rangaswamy's historic six and a landmark draw against West Indies
Article Text:
Shantha Rangaswamy's six that made history in India's first women's Test

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Indian team: Sandhya Mazumdar, Shobha Pandit, Fowzieh Khalili, Sudha Shah, Shantha Rangaswamy, Ujwala Nikam, Shubhangi Kulkarni, Susan Itticheria, Diana Edulji, Sharmila Chakraborty, Behroze Edulji.

Brief scores: West Indies: 274 in 78.4 overs (Louise Browne 28, Gloria Gill 53, Patricia Whittaker 32, Yolande Geddes-Hall 44, Leila Williams 43; Diana Edulji 2-48, Shubhangi Kulkarni 5-48) and 175/7 declared in 64.5 overs (Patricia 29, Leila 56; Sharmila Chakraborty 2-32, Shubhangi 2-28) drew with India: 269/6 declared in 99 overs (Shobha Pandit 69, Fowzieh Khalili 39, Shantha Rangaswamy 74, Shubhangi 26 not out; Leila Williams 2-50, Vivalyn Latty-Scott 3-51) and 30/1 in 17 overs.

BENGALURU: Women’s cricket in India has had its share of twists and turns. Its journey into Test cricket was no different. Although cricket had been introduced in the country much earlier, the first women’s national championship was held only in April 1973. The game was still finding its feet, with teams playing two and three-day red-ball matches. An Australian team toured India in 1975, and in February the following year, India travelled to New Zealand for a five-match ‘Test series’, which was subsequently deemed unofficial.The first women’s Test, between Australia and England, had been played in Brisbane in 1934. India had to wait another 42 years to make its official debut. That moment unfolded at the KSCA Stadium (renamed the M Chinnaswamy Stadium in 1987), when India hosted West Indies in the first of a six-Test series in October 1976.Led by Louise Browne, the visiting side took on Shantha Rangaswamy’s India in a three-day contest that began on October 31. For the women cricketers, it was a landmark moment.Recalling the occasion, Shantha said: “We had already played a couple of series against Australia and New Zealand, which were later deemed unofficial.So, we weren’t sure until later whether this match would count as an official one.”With one section of the stadium under renovation, the remaining stands were packed, with more than 22,000 spectators turning up. India’s line-up featured some of the rising stars of the game, including Diana Edulji, Shubhangi Kulkarni and Ujwala Nikam.Among those soaking in the atmosphere was former Indian wicketkeeper Kalpana Venkatachar, then a Karnataka age-group cricketer. She was part of a group of young women cricketers who volunteered at the match, handing out scorecards to spectators.“Back in the day, spectators also did the scoring. They watched, tracked and recorded every ball and run in a booklet provided to them. Our job was to hand out these booklets. The excitement was infectious and the crowd was boisterous,” Kalpana recalled.West Indies, who batted first, were bowled out for 274 in 78.4 overs. Shubhangi, one of India’s finest spinners, returned figures of 5/48, while Diana picked up two wickets.India’s reply produced two memorable knocks. Opener Shobha Pandit scored 69, but it was skipper Shantha’s gritty 74 that stole the show. Her innings also featured a landmark moment — a six over long-on off Patricia Whittaker, the first maximum by an Indian woman in international cricket and the first at the stadium. The stand where the ball landed has since been named after Shantha.She remembers the innings as an attempt to inject a modern-day T20 flavour into a game that was still played over three days.“With the matches being held over three days, most of them would end in draws. But I wanted to make it interesting and score some quick runs, like they do in T20 cricket now,” she said.India were 269/6 overnight after 99 overs and were looking to add to their total on the final morning. But an unexpected turn of events prompted Shantha to declare.“We came out to bat on the final day only to see wet patches on the pitch. This drew suspicion from the visiting side and the start was delayed. So, I declared in the hope that we could bowl them out.”West Indies declared their second innings at 175/7, setting India a target of 181. The hosts finished on 30/1 at stumps as the historic contest ended in a draw.For Kalpana and the other youngsters watching from the stands, however, the result was secondary. The sight of Shantha clearing the ropes had left a lasting impression.“Watching Shantha score a six made us believe that we could go the distance too,” she said.Indian women have played 42 more Tests in the five decades since that landmark outing. But the first, played in front of a packed crowd, remains special. The series ended in a 1-1 draw with four drawn contests.
Article Summary: West Indies bowled out for 274 in 78.4 overs. India declared on 269/6 overnight. Shantha Rangaswamy scored 74 not out. Shubhangi Kulkarni took 5/48. Diana Edulji took 2-48.

Article Title: Ryan Rickelton, Wiaan Mulder hundreds put South Africa in driver's seat, set 288-run target for Australia in series decider
Article Text:
South Africa's Ryan Rickelton celebrates his hundred with his teammate Wiaan Mulder (AP/PTI)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Centuries from Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder put South Africa in a commanding position against Australia in the series-deciding third Test at Newlands on Friday, setting up an intriguing final day's play.South Africa, who began the fourth day with a slender 40-run lead and six wickets in hand, finished their second innings on 387, stretching their advantage to 287 runs. Australia now need 288 on the final day to win the three-Test series, which is currently level at 1-1.Rickelton (101 off 219 balls) and Mulder (115 off 221 balls) led South Africa's recovery with a crucial sixth-wicket partnership worth 154 runs. The pair spent nearly 54 overs together, frustrating the Australian bowlers and forcing the visitors to turn to as many as eight bowling options.South Africa were 140/4 overnight and lost Matthew Breetzke in the morning session, caught at fine leg off Pat Cummins. The Australian captain's breakthrough ended a wicketless spell of more than 62 overs stretching back to the first Test in Durban.Rickelton and Mulder then took charge, adding 92 runs during the second session without losing a wicket. Rickelton reached his half-century off 105 deliveries, while Mulder went into the tea break unbeaten on 46.Their partnership crossed the 100-run mark after 193 balls.Australia managed to slow the scoring after tea, conceding just 13 runs in 10 overs, but the South African duo continued to build their lead. Rickelton eventually completed his third Test century off 219 balls, striking 12 boundaries. It was also the first century by a South African batter at No. 6 in the third or fourth innings of a Test since 2022.The partnership ended in unfortunate fashion when Mulder ran out Rickelton after sending him back too late. South Africa then suffered a brief collapse, losing four wickets for just 16 runs, with Gerald Coetzee also falling to a run-out after a mix-up involving Mulder.With the lower order exposed, Mulder took responsibility and shifted gears. Having taken 138 balls to reach his first 50, he needed only another 66 deliveries for his second half-century. He brought up his fourth Test hundred off 204 balls and finished with 10 fours and four sixes before falling to Cummins in the deep while attempting a pull shot.Mitchell Starc was Australia's most successful bowler in the innings, claiming 3/65 to take his match tally to nine wickets.Australia face a challenging chase on the final day, with Newlands having witnessed a successful fourth-innings target of 331 only once, when Australia achieved it in 2002. South Africa will also draw confidence from a pitch expected to offer increasing assistance to spinners and the presence of an in-form Simon Harmer, who was rested earlier in the match.The visitors have the entire fifth day to chase 288 and clinch the series, while South Africa will look to defend their total.
Article Summary: South Africa finish their second innings on 387, stretching their advantage to 287 runs. Australia need 288 on the final day to win the three-Test series, which is currently level at 1-1. Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder led South Africa's recovery with a crucial sixth-wicket partnership worth 154 runs.

Article Title: 'Chasing big totals is good for cricket': Sanath Jayasuriya

MUMBAI: Sri Lankan batting great Sanath Jayasuriya has given a thumbs-up to the recent trend of teams chasing down big totals on flat pitches in white-ball cricket.Sri Lanka pulled off the second-highest successful chase in ODIs when they overhauled England's 429-run total in a Tri-Series match in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, on October 22."It's very good to see that it's happening and players are getting runs on the board and chasing it, which is good for cricket. Teams and players are getting more and more confident, and that is the key. Anything is possible these days, and it is good to see that teams are putting runs on the board and even chasing, but I can see that is also putting the bowlers under pressure," Jayasuriya told reporters at an event on Friday."It's been a lot of changes in the rules. New things have come up in cricket with new regulations, which are good for the game," he added.Asked about the supremely talented and explosive Abhishek Sharma , who smashed a 38-ball 113, including a 35-ball century, to help India win the third T20I at Wellington by six wickets, Jayasuriya said, "He has a long way to go, but it is a good future for India. Let him play his natural game and let him do his work, and it will be a good investment for Indian cricket.""He (Abhishek) is an all-round player. You cannot say anything in specific is strong — he is an all-round player. He can play in any part of the park, so that is a good thing," he added.Praising India's white-ball team, Jayasuriya said, "They are talented cricketers and are playing well. India has got the talent and is playing good cricket at the moment. There are quite a few Indian players who have been doing well. Good to see them.They are talented, work hard and are playing well."Asked about Sri Lanka's impressive performance in Pakistan in the Tri-Series — they won two of their four matches and qualified for the final, where they will face Pakistan on Saturday — Jayasuriya felt that the campaign would boost their confidence ahead of their white-ball tour of India in December."It's a good confidence (booster) for the Sri Lankan team, which is doing well before they come to India. The confidence is high, they are playing well, and I hope they will do well in India too," the former dashing left-hander, who also served as Sri Lanka's chief selector, said.Jayasuriya backed India to do well in the forthcoming ODI and Test series in New Zealand."They are going to do well for sure, but away from India they have always looked to do well, and it will be a good series," he said.
Article Summary: Sri Lanka pulled off the second-highest successful chase in ODIs when they overhauled England's 429-run total in a Tri-Series match in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, on October 22. "It's very good to see that it's happening and players are getting runs on the board and chasing it, which is good for cricket," he said.

Article Title: Best ever! From 14 medals to 114: How India achieved more with fewer athletes at the Asian Para Games
Article Text:
Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

From 14 medals to 114: India's remarkable rise

India's Asian Para Games record

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Smaller contingent, bigger return

Hangzhou vs Aichi-Nagoya

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Athletics powers India's medal surge

India's leading medal-winning sports in Asian Para Games 2026

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Multiple medallists underline India's depth

Paralympic progress provides the wider context

Fourth place sets a new benchmark

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

From 14 medals in 2010 to 114 in 2026, India’s remarkable rise continued in Aichi-Nagoya as a smaller contingent surpassed its previous best, achieved 30 gold medals and secured its highest-ever finish at the continental para-sport showpiece.India’s campaign at the Asian Para Games 2026 was a triumph that few would have predicted when the size of the contingent became known. With just 167 athletes travelling to Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, the prospect of repeating the 100-plus medal haul achieved at Hangzhou in 2023 appeared ambitious. The previous edition had seen India send more than 300 athletes to the competition, returning with a record 108 medals after subsequent revisions to the original tally.But the Indian contingent defied expectations, producing an even bigger return with significantly fewer athletes. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place, both the highest medal tally and the best finish in the country's history at the event.The numbers tell a compelling story of progress. India improved its medal tally for the fifth consecutive edition, added to its gold-medal record and finished ahead of South Korea, which had threatened to challenge its position in the final standings.More than the record itself, the achievement highlighted how far India's para-sport movement has travelled in 16 years — from a modest 14-medal return at the inaugural edition in 2010 to a fourth-place finish among Asia's leading para-sport nations.India's progress at the Asian Para Games has been steady, with each edition bringing a new high in the overall medal tally.At Guangzhou in 2010, India won 14 medals — one gold, four silver and nine bronze — to finish 15th. The 2014 edition in Incheon brought a substantial improvement, with the country collecting 33 medals, including three gold, but remaining 15th in the standings.The breakthrough arrived at Jakarta in 2018. India's medal tally rose to 72, comprising 15 gold, 24 silver and 33 bronze, while its position improved to ninth.Hangzhou in 2023 marked another major leap. India crossed the 100-medal barrier for the first time, initially returning with 111 medals before the tally was revised to 108 following a doping-related disqualification and a medal reallocation. The revised haul comprised 27 gold, 32 silver and 49 bronze, with India eventually classified sixth.Aichi-Nagoya extended that upward trajectory. India added six medals to its revised Hangzhou total, increased its gold-medal count from 27 to 30 and climbed two places to fourth.The numbers at a glance: India's medal tally increased more than eightfold between 2010 and 2026. Its gold-medal count grew from one to 30, while its position improved from 15th to fourth.The rise has not been limited to the overall tally. India has improved its standing in three successive editions since 2014, moving from 15th to ninth, then sixth and now fourth. The 2026 result represents the culmination of a sustained upward trend rather than an isolated breakthrough.The most striking feature of India's latest performance was the efficiency with which its athletes converted participation into medals.India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi-Nagoya. That was considerably fewer than the 309 athletes listed for the Hangzhou campaign in 2023, yet the team surpassed its previous best by six medals.The comparison is revealing. India sent approximately 46 per cent fewer athletes than it did to Hangzhou, but its medal tally increased by nearly six per cent. The gold-medal count rose by three, the silver tally by three, and the bronze count remained unchanged.On a simple medals-per-athlete measure, India's return increased from approximately 0.35 medals per athlete in Hangzhou to 0.68 in Aichi-Nagoya. This is an aggregate comparison, not an individual success rate, since athletes can win multiple medals and the number of events and opportunities varies across sports.Nevertheless, the figures underline the scale of the achievement. A smaller squad did not merely match the previous edition's success; it established a new benchmark for Indian para-sport.Para-athletics was the backbone of India's campaign, delivering 65 medals — 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. That represented nearly 57 per cent of the country's overall tally and made athletics the single biggest contributor to India's fourth-place finish.Para-badminton followed with 16 medals, including three gold, five silver and eight bronze. Together, athletics and badminton accounted for 81 medals, more than 70 per cent of India's total.Swimming contributed 11 medals, comprising three silver and eight bronze. Archery added six medals, including three gold and three silver, while shooting produced five, with two gold, two silver and one bronze.Athletics' contribution also illustrates how India's progress has accelerated. At Hangzhou, para-athletics produced 52 medals, including 16 gold, 17 silver and 19 bronze. In Aichi-Nagoya, the discipline's haul rose to 65, with six additional gold medals.Badminton's contribution was different. India won 21 medals in the sport at Hangzhou, including four gold, but finished with 16 in 2026. Instead, the substantial gains in athletics and the contributions from other sports helped compensate for the decline in badminton medals.That distinction matters: the record haul reflects both the strength of India's established medal-winning disciplines and the need to broaden its success across events in future editions.India's record was supported by athletes who delivered more than once during the competition. A total of 26 Indian athletes won multiple medals, while six athletes collected multiple gold medals, demonstrating the importance of individual excellence in a campaign involving 11 sports.Archer Sheetal Devi was among the standout performers, winning two gold medals and a silver. Her two golds came in the mixed compound and individual compound events, while the silver added to her three-medal haul.Athletics provided several other multiple gold medallists. Dilip Gavit, Nishad Kumar, Pranav Soorma and Simran Sharma each won two gold medals, while shooting contributed through Mona Agarwal, who also secured two golds.Four athletes finished with three medals apiece: Sheetal Devi in archery, Thulasimathi Murugesan in badminton, Ravi Budigina in swimming and Himanshu Nandal in swimming. Their performances illustrated how athletes winning across multiple events can make a significant difference to a country's final tally.The figures also invite comparison with Hangzhou, where 25 Indian athletes won multiple medals. The increase to 26 in 2026 was modest, but the overall tally improved despite a much smaller contingent. The result points to a campaign in which medal-winning performances were concentrated among a relatively small squad.India's rise at the Asian Para Games has coincided with a significant improvement at the Paralympics, strengthening the country's standing in international para-sport.At Rio 2016, India won four medals and finished 43rd. Tokyo 2020 marked a breakthrough, with 19 medals — five gold, eight silver and six bronze — lifting India to 24th. At Paris 2024, India recorded its best Paralympic haul of 29 medals, comprising seven gold, nine silver and 13 bronze, to finish 18th.The progression at the Paralympics mirrors the broader trend at the Asian Para Games: larger medal returns, more gold medals and improvements in the standings.India's able-bodied contingent had also finished fourth at the 2026 Asian Games, although its 85-medal tally was below the 106 medals achieved at Hangzhou in 2023. The para contingent's performance offered a contrasting story of growth, with its medal count rising and its position improving.China dominated Aichi-Nagoya, finishing with 435 medals, including 207 gold. Hosts Japan were second with 186 medals, while Uzbekistan finished third with 145. India placed fourth with 114, ahead of South Korea, which collected 100 medals, including 29 gold.India's final position was not guaranteed until the closing stages. South Korea remained within reach, but its final-day return of one gold and two silver left it one gold behind India. The Indian contingent held on to fourth place with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze.The gap to third-placed Uzbekistan shows that further progress will require India to expand its medal-winning strength across disciplines. Yet the immediate achievement is significant: India has moved from 15th at the first two editions to fourth, while increasing its tally at every successive Games.The challenge now is to sustain that momentum, build a deeper pool of competitive athletes and reduce dependence on a handful of disciplines.For a contingent of just 167 athletes, 114 medals represent more than a record. They mark the latest step in a 16-year transformation of Indian para-sport — one that began with 14 medals in Guangzhou and has now culminated in a historic fourth-place finish in Aichi-Nagoya.
Article Summary: India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi- Nagoya. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place. It is the best finish in the country's history at the event.
